justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish baseline for what appears to be an asset trading near the 298–300 level. At the one-day horizon, I anchored close to the last observed price around 298.5, expecting very little net movement over such a short window. Mean reversion tendencies and the absence of any imminent scheduled catalyst suggested the price would stay close to its current level. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to 299.5, reflecting a mild drift assumption consistent with a modest upward bias in the underlying trend, while acknowledging that over five trading days there is enough time for modest trend continuation or minor news-driven moves. At the one-month horizon, the estimate rises to 302, which incorporates a slightly stronger trend assumption while remaining conservative — essentially saying the asset drifts a few points higher over roughly twenty trading days if conditions stay broadly stable.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to reflect how uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the 90% interval of roughly plus or minus six to seven points reflects typical short-run volatility — essentially one to two standard deviations of daily price movement scaled for intraday-to-close dynamics. At one week, the interval widens to roughly plus or minus twelve to thirteen points, capturing the accumulation of daily variance across five sessions. By one month, the interval spans about fifty-two points, reflecting that over twenty or so trading days, compounding volatility, macro surprises, and sentiment shifts can meaningfully move prices in either direction. The widths also bake in some fat-tail adjustment beyond pure Gaussian scaling.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected deterioration in macroeconomic data — such as a weaker-than-expected jobs report, an inflation surprise, or a central bank policy shift — could drive a sharp selloff well below the lower bound of the one-month interval. Geopolitical flare-ups or financial contagion from stress in credit markets could similarly produce outsized moves. On the upside, a strongly positive earnings season, a dovish policy pivot, or resolution of a geopolitical risk could drive prices meaningfully above 328 at the one-month horizon.

Finally, model risk itself is a source of tail exposure I should acknowledge. My estimates assume a relatively stable volatility regime, but if realized volatility spikes — as it can during liquidity crises or unexpected macro shocks — the true distribution of outcomes would have much fatter tails than my intervals imply. Conversely, if the market enters an unusually calm, low-volatility period, the actual range of outcomes could be considerably narrower than stated.
